planting.note: Soak seed overnight to soften the hard coat, then scatter on the soil surface after fall rains, barely covering it; sow in place, since the plant resents root disturbance.

directions: Cream-to-peach, translucent-petaled flowers with conspicuous orange throat veins bloom January through May on this cool-season desert annual, which is notable for its tight ecological tie to the specialist bee genus Xeralictus and as a larval host for a noctuid moth — a genuinely different pollinator story than the garden's existing hawkmoth-pollinated Mentzelia. Use a lean, gritty, rocky-to-sandy mix and never fertilize. Once established it self-sows readily into any bare, sun-baked gap, making it a good companion for other Mojave and Sonoran annuals in a gravel garden.

planting.note: Soak seed 24 hours and scatter onto lean, disturbed, sandy-to-rocky ground, left uncovered or barely covered; avoid organically rich beds, which favor weeds over this species.

directions: Bright yellow, sometimes red-based petals up to half an inch wide carry a glossy sheen that gives this Mojave Desert species its common name, and it supports an unusually broad pollinator resume — dozens of native bee species plus shared pollinators with citrus and safflower crops. Sow in early spring once soil temperatures reach 60-70°F, or in fall in true desert climates. It intergrades with closely related species in the wild, so seed-grown plants may show minor variation in petal size and leaf lobing.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or fall into lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; thin or space seedlings generously, since height varies widely with rainfall.

directions: Shiny yellow, five-petaled flowers each marked with a distinctive orange basal spot and often a notched petal tip give this species a comet-like look, native to scrub, woodland, and desert sand habitats across southern California, Arizona, Nevada, and Baja California. It tolerates slightly more organic content in the seedbed than many desert annuals without collapsing, but still fails in heavy or waterlogged soil. It works well mixed into a southern California or low-desert annual wildflower seed blend rather than grown as a single-species block.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall where winters are mild, or in early spring with cold exposure where winters are hard, into loamy-to-sandy or rocky soil; give it the sunniest, driest spot available.

directions: The widest-ranging small-flowered blazingstar, found from British Columbia to California to the Dakotas, this species occupies an unusually broad span of plant communities from chaparral and foothill woodland up into lodgepole, red fir, and subalpine forest margins. It is the most soil-tolerant species of the group, growing in open ground within woodland duff as well as pure mineral scree. Leave seed capsules in place through late summer so the barbed, Velcro-like hairs on the leaves can carry seed into bare disturbed patches.

planting.note: Sow in situ onto sandy, loamy, or rocky soil in full sun, uncovered or barely covered; thrives in disturbed ground like roadcuts and freshly scraped beds.

directions: Named for its noticeably white, round stem, this slender annual carries small yellow-to-orange star flowers from February through August depending on elevation, one of the longest bloom windows in the genus. Its wide elevational range from sea level to 7,000 feet across California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, and Washington makes it adaptable to a broader swath of gardens than the strict low-desert species. A deliberately under-mulched, under-irrigated corner of the garden suits it better than a tended border.
